title: How Do the Latest Black Sea Attacks Affect Global Food Security?
gist: Mutual Russian and Ukrainian attacks on Black Sea and Sea of Azov ports have simultaneously taken roughly 70 percent of Russia's and 90 percent of Ukraine's grain export capacity offline during peak wheat export season, pushing CBOT wheat futures to their highest since 2023. The shock lands on top of an 11 percent decline in production among the top seven wheat exporters and a Strait of Hormuz closure that is squeezing fertilizer supply.

insights.claim: Russian and Ukrainian strikes have for the first time simultaneously disabled both countries' grain export channels, removing an estimated 70 percent of Russia's grain export capacity and roughly 90 percent of Ukraine's grain shipments in the same season.
insights.so_what: Roughly 27 percent of world wheat exports sit behind a two-sided blockade; wheat-linked longs and food-import-dependent sovereigns are directly exposed.
insights.quote: Ukraine’s attacks, particularly on Russia’s ports in the Sea of Azov and at Novorossiysk, have removed an estimated 70 percent of Russia’s grain export capacity.
insights.locator: Q2: What are the impacts of recent attacks
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Vessel traffic through Ukraine's Black Sea ports has largely halted since July 22, 2026, cutting Ukrainian grain exports 75 percent in the first two weeks of August versus 2025 levels.
insights.so_what: A datable stop-date gives a clean marker for when the wheat price impulse began; watch weekly Ukrainian export prints for any restart.
insights.quote: vessel traffic through Black Sea ports has largely halted since July 22, causing grain exports to drop 75 percent in the first two weeks of August compared to 2025 levels.
insights.locator: Because of Russia’s attacks on grain-carrying ships
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Ukraine's August 12, 2026 strike on Novorossiysk halted all three of the port's grain terminals, leaving the secondary port of Tuapse as Russia's only operational Black Sea outlet.
insights.so_what: Novorossiysk handles 40 percent of Russian grain exports; its restart or continued outage is the single highest-leverage variable for wheat supply.
insights.quote: At time of writing, Russia’s only operational port on the Black Sea is the secondary port of Tuapse.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s August 12 strike on Novorossiysk
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Ukrainian forces attacked 76 vessels between July 6 and July 11, 2026, and Russia has attacked at least 57 cargo vessels in the Black Sea since June, marking the first confirmed Ukrainian assaults on ships carrying Russian grain.
insights.so_what: Commercial hull and war-risk insurance premia for Black Sea transits should reprice sharply; freight costs are now a structural cost in grain basis.
insights.locator: Since June, Russia has attacked at least 57 cargo vessels
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Ukrainian drone reach has expanded beyond the Black Sea to Russia's Baltic ports, including a September 2026 strike on Ust-Luga, a major fertilizer export terminal, and to the Caspian Sea.
insights.so_what: The supposed safe fallback route for Russian grain and fertilizer is itself now in range, so Baltic rerouting does not de-risk the trade.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s recent attacks have also demonstrated an expanded reach
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Russian wheat exports in August 2026 are estimated at 1.5-3.0 million metric tons against a recent August average of 5 million tons, implying as much as a 70 percent month-on-month collapse.
insights.so_what: A concrete tonnage gap to model into global balance sheets rather than a vague disruption narrative.
insights.locator: In recent years, Russia has exported an average of 5 million tons
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Analysts forecast Russia's July-September 2026 wheat exports at 5.6 million tons, roughly half the 11.3 million tons shipped in the same window a year earlier.
insights.so_what: A ~5.7 million ton quarterly shortfall from the world's top exporter is the core bullish input for wheat futures.
insights.locator: Analysts forecast Russia’s July–September wheat export volumes
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Ukraine's August 2026 grain exports are expected to run at roughly one-third of August 2025 levels.
insights.so_what: Compounds the Russian shortfall in the same weeks, removing the usual offset between the two suppliers.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s August grain exports are expected to be approximately one-third
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Russian rerouting through Baltic terminals plus Estonian and Latvian ports could carry roughly 10 million metric tons, about one-fifth of the 46 million tons Russia exported via Azov and Black Sea ports in the 2025-2026 season.
insights.so_what: Caps how much of the lost volume can return; the residual 80 percent gap is the durable part of the supply shock.
insights.locator: Grain shipments through Russia’s Baltic Sea terminals
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Ukraine's agriculture minister says fully operational alternative routes by rail, road and the Danube could move only half the volume its disrupted Black Sea ports handled.
insights.so_what: Even a best-case Ukrainian workaround leaves half its export capacity stranded, so the bullish wheat case does not need continued escalation.
insights.locator: According to Ukraine’s agriculture minister, alternative routes
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Record-low Danube water levels from extreme heat and low rainfall are cutting cargo capacity and creating transit queues in which higher-priced cargo such as fuel is prioritized over grain.
insights.so_what: Climate is compounding the military disruption; grain loses the allocation fight against fuel on the one remaining river route.
insights.locator: Today, extreme heat and low rainfall have dropped Danube River levels
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Russia has suspended export duties on wheat, barley and corn through the end of 2026 to offset the higher trading costs of rerouting.
insights.so_what: A fiscal subsidy to keep Russian grain price-competitive despite logistics costs; signals Moscow expects the disruption to persist.
insights.locator: To ease the impacts of high trading costs
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Prolonged export blockage could cause up to $3 billion in losses for Ukraine's agriculture sector and create a second-order hit to future harvests as unsold inventory fills storage and starves farmers of planting capital.
insights.so_what: The supply shock is not one-season; a capital-starved Ukrainian planting campaign extends the deficit into 2027-2028.
insights.locator: Recent disruptions could cause up to $3 billion in losses
insights.speaker: CSIS

themes.theme: Global wheat supply squeeze beyond the war

insights.claim: Benchmark wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade have reached their highest levels since 2023 on the back of the Black Sea attacks.
insights.so_what: The tradable expression of the shock is already in motion; the question is persistence, not direction.
insights.quote: The recent attacks have caused benchmark wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade to reach their highest levels since 2023.
insights.locator: Q4: How could recent attacks affect global agriculture markets
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: USDA projects combined production of the world's top seven wheat exporters will fall 11 percent in 2026/2027 and their exports 7 percent, meaning the Black Sea disruption is layered onto an already-shrinking global supply base.
insights.so_what: Removes the usual buffer of substitute origins; there is no slack exporter to fill the Russian and Ukrainian gap.
insights.locator: These disruptions are coinciding with a decline in global wheat production
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: U.S. wheat production is expected to fall 26 percent to its lowest level since the 1970-1971 season, with exports down almost 15 percent.
insights.so_what: The traditional swing supplier is itself in deficit, which is the least-priced leg of the wheat bull case.
insights.quote: wheat production is expected to fall by 26 percent, representing the lowest wheat production levels since 1970–1971
insights.locator: In the United States, wheat production is expected to fall
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: FAO data show world wheat prices were 15 percent higher in August 2026 than a year earlier, though aggregate cereal prices remain well below the 2022 peak.
insights.so_what: Calibrates the move as significant but not yet crisis-level, leaving room for further upside if the blockade persists.
insights.locator: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN Food Price Index
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Elevated cereal prices would hit net-food-importing countries hardest, cutting consumption of both staples and more expensive nutritious foods simultaneously, as in 2022.
insights.so_what: Points at sovereign and FX stress in food-importing EMs and at political instability risk as the downstream trade.
insights.locator: As in 2022, elevated global food prices would hit
insights.speaker: CSIS

themes.theme: Hormuz spillover into fertilizer and tactics

insights.claim: A UK-based research institute argues Iran's threats to safe passage in the Strait of Hormuz may be normalizing the targeting of civilian vessels, plausibly informing Russia's decision to accelerate attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea.
insights.so_what: Chokepoint coercion is becoming a transferable playbook, raising war-risk pricing across all maritime chokepoints, not just the one in the headlines.
insights.quote: may be normalizing the targeting of civilian vessels
insights.locator: According to one UK-based research institute
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Destruction of energy infrastructure and shipping delays in the Persian Gulf drove North American fertilizer prices up 30 percent versus prewar by April 2026 before easing, and led some farmers to plant fewer acres of fertilizer-intensive crops including wheat.
insights.so_what: A direct mechanism linking Middle East energy disruption to next year's wheat supply; fertilizer prices are a leading indicator for grain.
insights.locator: By April 2026, North American fertilizer prices had increased 30 percent
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Although 84 percent of Russia's mineral fertilizer exports move through the Baltic Sea, its Black Sea fertilizer exports from Novorossiysk and Taman have effectively halted since the escalation, while Ukraine has proven it can reach Baltic ports too.
insights.so_what: Global fertilizer supply now has correlated exposure to both the Gulf and the Baltic; a Ust-Luga outage would be the tail event to hedge.
insights.quote: Though 84 percent of Russia’s mineral fertilizer exports are through the Baltic Sea
insights.locator: Likewise, the concurrence of the Strait of Hormuz closure
insights.speaker: CSIS

themes.theme: Why no grain deal is coming

insights.claim: Ukraine proposed on August 13, 2026 that both sides halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea and Russia dismissed it the next day, with Moscow insisting any maritime ceasefire also cover its energy infrastructure while continuing strikes on Ukraine's energy system.
insights.so_what: Removes the near-term de-escalation scenario from the price path; the counteroffer structure makes a deal unlikely without broader terms.
insights.locator: On August 13, Ukraine proposed to Russia
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Neither side is likely to revive a Black Sea Grain Initiative-style regime because Ukraine's exports actually rose after the BSGI ended and its inspections let Russia throttle Ukrainian shipments, while Russia considered the deal one-sided.
insights.so_what: Markets anchoring on a 2022-style diplomatic fix are mispricing; the historical precedent argues against repetition, not for it.
insights.locator: In 2022, the establishment of the BSGI
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Grain industry analysts fear the Black Sea hostilities could last as long as the Russia-Ukraine war itself, with expanding effects on agricultural markets, while Turkey has drafted an unadopted safe-passage plan.
insights.so_what: Frames the disruption as a multi-year regime change in grain logistics rather than a spike to fade.
insights.quote: recent hostilities in the Black Sea could last as long as the Russia-Ukraine war itself
insights.locator: Absent a ceasefire, grain industry analysts fear
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Ukraine's own naval strike capability, not diplomacy, has been the decisive variable for its exports: after forcing Russia's Black Sea Fleet to relocate to Novorossiysk in 2023, Ukraine's self-declared corridor moved roughly 100 million metric tons of grain through January 2026.
insights.so_what: Track Ukrainian naval and drone capability, not ceasefire headlines, as the leading indicator for whether grain flows resume.
insights.locator: Since Ukraine launched the Ukrainian Corridor in September 2023
insights.speaker: CSIS
